summary: Weekly POC sync to review latency regression after moving to 8k token sequences. Main focus: TTFT regressions on cold starts, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, kernel choices (fused attention vs matmul path), and sequence-length dependent batching. Action items defined to run targeted benchmarks and share tuning docs.
transcript: 09:30 Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check-in, we got 45 minutes, we'll start with what we saw in the benchmarks this week.

09:31 Sam Torres: Yeah morning. so we bumped the seq_len to 8k to support longer context and we noticed TTFT bumped, like median went from ~110ms to ~190ms on the hosted route. tail also got worse, 95th from 450 to 720 ms.
09:32 Priya Patel: ok thanks for the numbers. couple quick clarifying q's — were those cold starts (no prefix cache) or warmed KV cache? and were you using streaming=true?
09:33 Sam Torres: mostly cold, we did one run warmed but it's flaky; streaming was on but with 256 token chunks. sorry, i shoulda put that in the sheet, my bad.

09:34 Jordan Lee: it's cool. that aligns with what we saw in the internal logs — TTFT tends to spike on cold KV/cache and larger seq_len because the kernel path chooses a different attention implementation for >4k tokens.
09:35 Lina Chen: yeah that's our worry — we can't add a huge warmup overhead for every request, customers expect sub-200ms first token for chat flows. any suggestions?

09:36 Priya Patel: a few. first, streaming chunk size: 256 is small for 8k contexts; overhead per chunk adds. bump to 512 or 1024 depending on your desired granularity — that drops TTFT for the first chunk because we can pipeline better. second, kernel choice: the runtime switches to a fused-attn kernel at longer seqs which is faster for throughput but higher startup cost. we can force the matmul path for TTFT-sensitive endpoints.
09:37 Marcus Doyle: clarify "force matmul" what does that mean operationally? will that hurt throughput?

09:38 Priya Patel: yeah, forcing the matmul path reduces the per-request startup because we avoid some compilation and memory prep that fused-attn does. throughput may be lower for very large batches, but for single-request latency it's usually better. we can expose that as a kernel_preference flag for your dedicated pool or route.
09:39 Sam Torres: are there numbers? like how big is the TTFT delta?

09:40 Priya Patel: in our lab: 4k->8k on fused path median TTFT went from ~120ms to ~210ms, while matmul forced stayed ~140ms. 95th also improved by ~200ms. however throughput tested with 16 concurrent streams favored fused-attn for tokens/sec.

09:41 Jordan Lee: also quantization affects this — you mentioned you're running q4_0 VM quant; the kernel selection sometimes picks a slower kernel on q4 models due to memory layout. Priya, we should recommend quant profile that balances TTFT.
09:42 Priya Patel: agreed. for RiverMark's use-case (low concurrency, interactive chat), q4_0 with matmul path or q8_0 with fused-attn may be the sweet spots. we'll provide two config snapshots.
09:43 Lina Chen: about cache warmup — can we do a lightweight prefix cache priming? we have predictable system prompts so maybe pre-warm key pages overnight.

09:44 Priya Patel: yes, prefix/KV cache priming is effective. if you have a routing policy that pins certain customer IDs to a pool, we can schedule a background priming job that touches the KV bits on container start so cold starts are rarer. cost tradeoff is extra requests but small compared to latency wins.
09:45 Sam Torres: we can do that. what's the recommended priming pattern? how many tokens?
09:46 Priya Patel: prime the common prefixes, around 512-1k tokens per persona. the runtime keeps KV pages and subsequent requests avoid the heavy startup. i'll add a snippet to the notes.

09:47 Jordan Lee: another quick item — streaming toggles also affect client behavior. if you increase chunk size, the perceived responsiveness might be slightly lumpier for long responses. did we try client-side partial render?
09:48 Sam Torres: our frontend already handles partial renders, but product wants the first token <150ms ideally. so we need the backend change more than frontend tricks.

09:49 Priya Patel: final thing: profiling. we need trace logs from a representative cold-run and a warmed-run. Sam, can you attach perf logs (kernel selection trace + NVTX) to the shared benchmark sheet? that'll let us pinpoint where the extra ms are spent (compilation, memory copy, attention kernel).
09:50 Sam Torres: yes i'll run the harness this afternoon. one question — on dedicated vs hosted: if we move this route to a dedicated pool with pinned GPUs, would that reduce these cold TTFT spikes?

09:51 Jordan Lee: typically yes; dedicated gives warmer caches because the containers are long-lived and you avoid multi-tenant eviction. also you get kernel caching across processes. but it's a cost tradeoff. we can model cost/latency for you.
09:52 Marcus Doyle: can you show the cost delta? we have budget constraints for Q1.

09:53 Jordan Lee: we'll include a cost delta in the updated benchmark spreadsheet — showing hosted with priming, hosted without priming, and dedicated pool numbers with expected monthly $/token and latency percentiles.

09:54 Priya Patel: for immediates, we'll share a kernel selection guide: commands to force matmul vs fused, suggested quant profiles for TTFT, streaming chunk sizes (512/1024), and a priming job template. also we'll propose a small AB test: 10% of traffic forced-matmul to verify product metrics.
09:55 Sam Torres: tasty. last bit — security question: if we do priming, how do we ensure no customer PII is stored in cache?

09:56 Priya Patel: good call. priming should use synthetic or redacted prompts; we can use hashed identifiers and ensure KMS encryption + retention TTLs. we'll include security notes and the SOC2 doc link in the share.

09:57 Jordan Lee: okay, recap of next steps: Jordan uploads updated benchmark + cost model, Priya shares kernel guide & priming template, Sam runs 1k streaming tests and shares logs. we'll reconvene same time next week. thanks everyone.
09:58 Marcus Doyle: thanks, great recap. bye.
09:59 Aisha Gomez: thanks all — I'll send the calendar invite for the kernel deep dive next week. bye.
